title: The Arcades and the Border: from the Berlin childhood to the niche at Portbou
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Berlin-Tiergarten, the birth on Magdeburger Platz
stops.date_confidence: attested. Deutsche Biographie's authority record and German Wikipedia both give 15 July 1892 and the Tiergarten district. The pin is Magdeburger Platz as geocoded by Nominatim; the pool's original coordinate fell some 700 metres short of the square and is not used.
stops.campa: Walter Bendix Schönflies Benjamin is born in the Tiergarten district of west Berlin, first child of Emil Benjamin, a dealer in art and antiques turned investor, and Pauline née Schönflies. The family is Jewish, assimilated, prosperous. The household runs on servants, carpets, telephones, and the confidence of the imperial capital in its own arrangements; a brother, Georg, and a sister, Dora, follow. He will spend his working life writing about interiors, thresholds, and the objects a bourgeois childhood arranges around a child. He is born inside one.
suggested_refs: Berliner Kindheit um neunzehnhundert, the Tiergarten and Charlottenburg pieces

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the streets of the childhood
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The childhood geography of Tiergarten and Charlottenburg is attested in general terms, but no single confirmed address supports this stop and the date is a placement inside the 1890s rather than a record of anything.
stops.campa: No single address is recorded for any of it; the geography that survives is the quarter. Thirty-five years later, already in exile, he sets it down as Berliner Kindheit um neunzehnhundert, a childhood assembled out of objects and thresholds instead of a life story. The child is walked through Charlottenburg and the Tiergarten by servants and by his mother: shop windows, courtyards, the loggias at the back of the apartment blocks, the telephone in the hall, the pantry, the reading of street names off their enamel plates.
suggested_refs: Berliner Kindheit um neunzehnhundert, written in exile from the 1930s

stops.name: Kaiser-Friedrich-Schule, Charlottenburg: eleven years of school
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for enrolment; the attachment to the school runs, with interruptions, to the Abitur in 1912. Month and day are not recorded and default to 01.
stops.campa: He enters the Kaiser-Friedrich-Schule in Charlottenburg at nine. Illness recurs and interrupts the terms. Conventional schooling he never comes to like, and the dislike hardens into a position he holds for life: that the German school is built to manufacture compliant adults out of children, and that a child's own experience is the thing it exists to overwrite. His marks stay good all the same, and nothing in the reports says what he is reading on his own. He remains attached to the place, on and off, until the Abitur in 1912.
suggested_refs: Benjamin's early essays in the youth-movement press on school reform

stops.name: Grunewald, the villa on Delbrückstraße
stops.date_confidence: the address, Delbrückstraße 23 in Berlin-Grunewald, is attested by German Wikipedia; the year is a placement inside the 1900s. The pin is Nominatim's geocoding of the house number; the pool's coordinate sat some 450 metres off and is not used. The house no longer stands.
stops.campa: The family occupies a substantial villa at Delbrückstraße 23 in Grunewald, out where Berlin's new money builds among the pines. Rooms, a garden, a staircase, a front door with its own protocol of admission: the furniture of the Berlin childhood book, written down from memory in exile after the house had ceased to be a place he could enter. The building no longer stands. What survives of it is an address and a prose reconstruction made by a man who could not go back.
stops.quote: its presence in time and space, its unique existence at the place where it happens to be
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935), trans. Harry Zohn, on what a reproduction cannot carry
suggested_refs: Delbrückstraße 23, Berlin-Grunewald, demolished

stops.name: Haubinda, the reform school and Gustav Wyneken
stops.date_confidence: attested; sources give the span 1905-1907. Month and day default to 01. A claim circulating in the source dossier that he already signed himself Ardor in these years could not be confirmed and is not carried here. The pin is Haubinda, a village of the municipality Westhausen in the Hildburghausen district; the pool's coordinate was roughly 45 kilometres wrong, near Suhl.
stops.campa: Sent away for his health to Hermann Lietz's country boarding school in the Thuringian hills, the boy falls under Gustav Wyneken, a teacher who tells his pupils that youth is not a waiting room for adulthood but a condition with its own authority. Benjamin takes it as doctrine, and will carry Wyneken's language into the Berlin student movement, publish in it, argue in it, and break with the man over the war. He is thirteen when he arrives. The stay runs from 1905 to 1907, and the vocabulary of it lasts him a decade longer.
suggested_refs: The Hermann-Lietz-Schule at Haubinda, Thuringia
Gustav Wyneken, Schule und Jugendkultur

segments.name: The Free Students and the War

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, the first semesters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1912 for the Abitur and the Freiburg matriculation; the semester is not fixed in the sources consulted and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Abitur in hand, he matriculates at the Albert-Ludwigs-Universität in Freiburg to read philosophy, German literature, and psychology, and sits in the lecture room of Heinrich Rickert, the neo-Kantian whose value-philosophy governs the southwest German schools. The town is small, the Black Forest starts at the edge of it, and the student is nineteen and already writing letters that are drafted like essays. The argument he wants is not happening here. Within the year he is back in Berlin.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Rickert's Freiburg lectures, 1912

stops.name: Berlin, the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität and the Free Students
stops.date_confidence: the Berlin enrolment period 1912-1915 is attested, as is his presidency of the Berlin Freie Studentenschaft. The exact term dates of the presidency are not fixed in the sources consulted; the year given here places it, and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: At the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität on Unter den Linden he hears Georg Simmel, the sociologist of money, of fashion, and of the mental life of the great city, and throws himself into the Freie Studentenschaft, the organized wing of Wyneken's youth movement. He is elected its Berlin president. Then the war comes and takes the movement apart from inside. The programme had been educational reform pursued as though it were a spiritual reform, and its enemy the professional careerism the university trains for.
suggested_refs: Benjamin's 1914-15 addresses to the Berlin Freie Studentenschaft

stops.name: Berlin, the death of Fritz Heinle
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested by German Wikipedia. The exact building is not identified in any source consulted and the pin is central Berlin, an approximation. The reading of the deaths as a protest against the war is what the surviving friends said; later biographers treat it as unresolved and this file leaves it unresolved.
stops.campa: On the eighth of August, five days after Germany declares war on France, the poet Fritz Heinle and Rika Seligson turn on the gas in the student meeting rooms and die there. Heinle is Benjamin's closest friend. The circle around them reads the deaths as a protest against the war; later biographers leave the reading open and the record does not close it. The youth movement Benjamin had led in Berlin does not survive the year. Neither does his attachment to Wyneken, who declares for the war.
suggested_refs: Heinle's unpublished poems, kept by Benjamin
Howard Eiland and Michael W. Jennings, Walter Benjamin: A Critical Life
sources: Peter Gordon, review of Eiland and Jennings, The New Republic

stops.name: Berlin, meeting Gershom Scholem
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1915 by both the English and German Wikipedia articles; month and day are not recorded and default to 01.
stops.campa: He meets Gerhard Scholem, later Gershom, a mathematics student five years younger who is teaching himself Hebrew and reading Kabbalah against the grain of a comfortably assimilated Berlin family much like his own. The friendship becomes the fixed point of Benjamin's intellectual life: twenty-five years of letters, arguments over Judaism and Marxism, and Scholem's standing invitation to come to Jerusalem, which Benjamin accepts in principle again and again and never once acts on.
stops.quote: the Jews represent an elite in the ranks of the spiritually active
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, Gesammelte Schriften II:839, quoted in Bernd Witte, Walter Benjamin: An Intellectual Biography; a mid-sentence fragment, addressee and year not established
suggested_refs: Gershom Scholem, Walter Benjamin: The Story of a Friendship
The Benjamin-Scholem correspondence, 1915-1940
sources: Bernd Witte, Walter Benjamin: An Intellectual Biography, via Open Library full-text search

stops.name: Munich, the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the move; the Munich period runs 1915-1917. Month and day default to 01, which puts this stop and the Scholem meeting on the same nominal date; both are dated only to 1915 in the sources.
stops.campa: He moves to Munich and enrolls at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität, working through phenomenology and classical philology while the war grinds on somewhere the seminar rooms do not mention. Scholem's letters follow him south. He writes the essay on language as such and on the language of man, in which naming is what language is for and communication is only what is left of it. The plan that closes the Munich period is simple and unheroic: marry, cross into neutral Switzerland before the army can reach him, and take a doctorate there while the war finishes without him.
suggested_refs: Benjamin's 1916 essay 'Über Sprache überhaupt und über die Sprache des Menschen'

segments.name: Switzerland, the Doctorate, and the Angel Bought in Munich

stops.name: Berlin, the marriage to Dora Sophie Kellner
stops.date_confidence: the date 17 April 1917 is attested. The place is not stated directly: the pool's chronology left it unspecified and guessed at Switzerland, but German Wikipedia's article on Dora Sophie Kellner has the couple marrying and only then going to Switzerland, which puts the wedding in Germany and most probably Berlin. The pin is central Berlin, not a sourced address.
stops.campa: He marries Dora Sophie Kellner on the seventeenth of April. She is a writer and a translator, sharp, and better than he is at earning money, which will matter for the next thirteen years and matter most bitterly at the end of them. Until recently she was married to Max Pollak. He is twenty-four. Immediately after the wedding the two of them leave Germany for Switzerland, where he is out of reach of his call-up, and no address is recorded for the ceremony they leave from.
suggested_refs: Dora Sophie Kellner's own journalism and translations of the 1920s

stops.name: Bern, the birth of Stefan Rafael
stops.date_confidence: attested. German Wikipedia's article on Dora Sophie Kellner gives 11 April 1918 at Bern; the pool's chronology carried only the bare year, which undersold an available precise date.
stops.campa: Stefan Rafael Benjamin is born at Bern on the eleventh of April. His father is twenty-five, a doctoral candidate in a neutral country living on money from Berlin, and he starts a notebook of the child's sentences: coinages, mishearings, private grammar, recorded for years as material rather than as sentiment. Whatever else the marriage becomes, the notebook does not stop. The war is two borders away and will end in November. Stefan will outlive both his parents and die in 1972.
suggested_refs: Benjamin's notebooks of Stefan's speech, published as Opinions et pensées

stops.name: Bern, the doctorate under Richard Herbertz
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1919 for the award; the Bern period runs 1917-1919. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Under Richard Herbertz at the University of Bern he completes Der Begriff der Kunstkritik in der deutschen Romantik, an argument that the Jena Romantics turned criticism into something other than judgment: the completion of the work, the medium in which a work goes on thinking after its author has stopped. It is the one unambiguous academic success of his life. Bern awards it summa cum laude in 1919, and no post follows, in Switzerland or anywhere else.
suggested_refs: Der Begriff der Kunstkritik in der deutschen Romantik, Bern 1919

stops.name: Grunewald, the return from Bern
stops.date_confidence: the return to Berlin in 1920 is attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. That the family stayed first at the writer Erich Gutkind's house is a reconstruction from German Wikipedia; Gutkind's exact Grunewald address is not established, and the pin repeats Delbrückstraße 23 rather than pretending to a second one.
stops.campa: The family comes back to Berlin and stays for a period at the house of the writer Erich Gutkind before Benjamin returns, at twenty-eight and with a wife and a child, to living inside his parents' money in Grunewald. The inflation is beginning and the fortune that made the villa possible is dissolving month by month. He is a doctor of philosophy with no employment and a plan to habilitate. The arguments with his father about all of this are constant and are recorded in the letters.
suggested_refs: The Benjamin-Scholem letters of 1920-21 on the household in Grunewald

stops.name: Berlin, Zur Kritik der Gewalt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1921; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He writes Zur Kritik der Gewalt. The essay separates the violence that founds a legal order from the violence that maintains one, shows the two feeding each other inside the institution of the police, and then points past both to what he calls divine violence, which founds no law and leaves no boundary stones. He does not say what any of that would look like on a street. Is the silence caution, or is it the thing the essay is for? A century of readers has not settled it, and the text gives them nothing to settle it with.
suggested_refs: Zur Kritik der Gewalt, Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, 1921

stops.name: Munich, buying the Angelus Novus
stops.date_confidence: year, city, price of 1000 marks, and gallery are attested; the month is not settled. German Wikipedia's Walter Benjamin article gives April 1921, its Angelus Novus article gives May or early June 1921, and the two are left standing against each other here. The pin is the Galerie Neue Kunst at the Odeonsplatz, where Hans Goltz traded from 1912; the firm moved to Briennerstraße only in 1928, after Goltz's death, so the pool's Briennerstraße coordinate is anachronistic.
stops.campa: At Hans Goltz's Galerie Neue Kunst, in the best position in the city right on the Odeonsplatz, he pays a thousand marks for a small monoprint Paul Klee had made the year before: a figure with raised wings, teeth showing, hair curling like scrolls of paper, called Angelus Novus. He carries it to every address he holds afterwards, Berlin, Paris, the rented rooms of the exile. Scholem writes a poem on it and Benjamin plans a journal named after it. Nineteen years later it becomes the angel of history.
stops.quote: His face is turned towards the past. Where we see the appearance of a chain of events, he sees one single catastrophe, which unceasingly piles rubble on top of rubble and hurls it before his feet.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'On the Concept of History' (1940), Thesis IX, on the Klee monoprint bought here in 1921; trans. Dennis Redmond, marxists.org
suggested_refs: Paul Klee, Angelus Novus, 1920, oil transfer and watercolour, now Israel Museum, Jerusalem
Verso Books, 'The Storm Blowing from Paradise: Walter Benjamin and Klee's Angelus Novus'
sources: Verso Books blog on the Angelus Novus provenance

stops.name: Capri, Bloch and Lukács and Asja Lācis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1924; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Poverty as much as anything sends him to Capri, where living is cheap and a German colony of writers has formed on the rock. He befriends Ernst Bloch, reads Georg Lukács's History and Class Consciousness, and meets Asja Lācis, a Latvian Bolshevik theatre director working on children's theatre, who is unimpressed by metaphysics and says so to his face. The habilitation on the German mourning play is drafted here. So is the turn toward Marxism that will strain the friendship with Scholem for the next sixteen years.
suggested_refs: Georg Lukács, Geschichte und Klassenbewusstsein, 1923

stops.name: Naples, the essay written with Asja Lācis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the essay Neapel; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: With Lācis he writes Neapel, a short essay built out of fragments instead of description: the porosity of the city, buildings never finished and never demolished, private life spilling out into the street, improvisation as the governing law of the place. The method is the finding. A city can be written as a montage of noticed things, and the noticing carries the argument without a thesis on top of it. It is the first rehearsal of a book about Paris he has not yet conceived.
suggested_refs: Walter Benjamin and Asja Lācis, 'Neapel', Frankfurter Zeitung, 1925
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Walter Benjamin' bibliography

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the habilitation withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: the withdrawal in 1925 is attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and by Wikipedia; the submission runs from 1923. Month and day default to 01. The pin is the coordinate already used for Frankfurt am Main elsewhere in the corpus; the habilitation itself was handled at the university's Bockenheim campus, roughly 50.1180, 8.6523.
stops.campa: He submits Ursprung des deutschen Trauerspiels to the University of Frankfurt: German baroque mourning plays read through allegory, ruin, and melancholy, opening with an epistemo-critical prologue on the idea as a constellation. The readers, Hans Cornelius and Franz Schultz among them, report that they cannot understand it, and let him know that withdrawal would be less humiliating than rejection. He is thirty-three, with a wife, a son, and no income of his own. He withdraws the thesis in 1925 and never holds a university post.
suggested_refs: Ursprung des deutschen Trauerspiels, submitted 1925, published as a book 1928
sources: University of Chicago Press excerpt on the Benjamin biography

stops.name: Moscow, the winter diary
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1926, with the stay running to February 1927; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He arrives in December for two winter months, officially on commission, actually to see Asja Lācis, who is ill in a sanatorium and does not give him the answer he came for. He keeps a diary: queues, snow, the price of things, the Party's tightening grip on what may be staged, the bureaucratic weather of a revolution eight years old. He weighs joining the Communist Party through the winter, writing about the decision the way other men write about choosing a city to live in, and does not join. He leaves in February.
stops.quote: The subject of historical cognition is the battling, oppressed class itself.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'On the Concept of History' (1940), Thesis XII, trans. Dennis Redmond, marxists.org
suggested_refs: Moskauer Tagebuch, published posthumously

segments.name: One-Way Street: the Arcades, the Microphone, the Divorce

stops.name: Paris, the arcades begin at the rue de Richelieu
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927 for the start of the project, first conceived with Franz Hessel; the work continues in this library until 1940. Month and day default to 01. The pin is the Bibliothèque nationale's Richelieu site, the only BnF reading room in existence in Benjamin's lifetime; the Tolbiac building did not open until 1996.
stops.campa: He begins, with Franz Hessel, notes for a short piece on the covered shopping arcades of the nineteenth century, and the notes do not stop. At the Bibliothèque nationale on the rue de Richelieu he reads himself into fashion, gaslight, panoramas, the flâneur, Haussmann, and Baudelaire, filing everything into lettered convolutes. The two men are already translating Marcel Proust into German together, so the Paris of involuntary memory stands behind the Paris of the arcades. No finished book ever comes of it. He is still filing in this room in 1940.
suggested_refs: Das Passagen-Werk, ed. Rolf Tiedemann, 1982
The Arcades Project, trans. Howard Eiland and Kevin McLaughlin, Harvard, 1999
sources: Nominatim geocoding of 58 rue de Richelieu

stops.name: Berlin, Einbahnstraße and the Trauerspiel book
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1928 for both books; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Two books appear in the same year from the same publisher. Ursprung des deutschen Trauerspiels comes out three years after the university refused it, and is seriously reviewed in the German press, and Benjamin is thirty-six and still without a salary. The other is Einbahnstraße, a sequence of short prose pieces named after signs, shops, filling stations, and street furniture. Its dedication says that Asja Lācis cut the street through the author the way an engineer cuts one through a city.
suggested_refs: Einbahnstraße, Rowohlt, 1928
Ursprung des deutschen Trauerspiels, Rowohlt, 1928

stops.name: Berlin, the microphone
stops.date_confidence: the broadcasting runs from 1927 to January 1933 and the year here places it in the middle; month and day default to 01. The pin is the Haus des Rundfunks on Masurenallee, which opens only in 1931, so Berlin broadcasts before that came from the Vox-Haus on Potsdamer Straße. The pool's coordinate corresponded to no broadcasting site at all.
stops.campa: From 1927 he works at the microphone: talks, book discussions, radio plays, and above all programmes for children, on Berlin street names and dialects, the history of toys, swindlers, and disasters. Some of them he calls Hörmodelle, listening models, small scenes staged to teach an audience how a situation actually works. It is the best-paid writing of his life and he treats it as writing rather than as filler. Roughly eighty scripts are associated with him. Almost none of the broadcasts themselves survive.
stops.quote: that which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935), trans. Harry Zohn
suggested_refs: Radio Benjamin, ed. Lecia Rosenthal, Verso
Haus des Rundfunks, Masurenallee 8-14, Berlin, opened 1931
sources: Nominatim geocoding of Haus des Rundfunks

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the second microphone
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the pin. The Frankfurt broadcasts of 1929-1932 are attested, but the exact broadcasting house could not be confirmed in this pass: the Südwestdeutsche Rundfunkdienst stood on the Eschersheimer Landstraße in the Nordend and the pin is a point on that street, not a sourced address. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The Frankfurt station takes him as well, and for four years he moves between two studios in two cities, writing to length and to the clock. The Frankfurt scripts carry the same repertoire under a different call sign: the listening models, the children's hours, the book talks. The station stands on the Eschersheimer Landstraße in the Nordend, at a house number nobody has since established. Between the two stations something near eighty broadcasts are logged from 1927 onward. In January 1933 the new government reorganizes German radio, and the work stops.
suggested_refs: The surviving Frankfurt radio scripts, 1929-1932

stops.name: Berlin, the divorce decree
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing. German Wikipedia's article on Dora Sophie Kellner gives 27 March 1930 for the decree, with Benjamin found at fault; its article on Walter Benjamin gives the looser April 1930, which is what the pool carried. The precise date is preferred here and the discrepancy is not resolved. The pin is a central Berlin approximation, not a sourced courthouse address.
stops.campa: The divorce from Dora is pronounced in Berlin after proceedings that ran for years and covered adultery, money, the custody of Stefan, and the books. Benjamin is found at fault. He loses part of the collection of children's books he had assembled over two decades, which for a man who wrote about book collecting as a passion bordering on an illness is the line on the settlement that stings. Dora will nevertheless house him at her Italian pension for years afterward.
stops.quote: Of all the ways of acquiring books, writing them oneself is regarded as the most praiseworthy method.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'Unpacking My Library: A Talk About Book Collecting' (1931), trans. Harry Zohn, in Illuminations
suggested_refs: 'Unpacking My Library', 1931
Benjamin's collection of children's books, dispersed in the settlement

stops.name: Sant Antoni de Portmany, Ibiza
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1932-1933 for the Ibiza stays; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He goes to Ibiza because it is the cheapest place a German with no income can live, and lodges in stretches near the household of Felix Noeggerath at Sant Antoni. There is no electricity where he sleeps and no running water. He is forty, and the profession he had made for himself has just been abolished in his own country. He writes autobiographical fragments, pieces of the Berlin childhood, short stories, and letters asking for money. He walks a great deal and notes what the peasants build and how they build it.
suggested_refs: The Ibiza sequences and 'Ibizenkische Folge', 1932

stops.name: Nice, the will and the chronicle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Nice suicide crisis of 1932 is reported by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and by Wikipedia, but the month is not fixed in the sources consulted and defaults to 01, which puts this stop on the same nominal date as the Ibiza stay of the same year.
stops.campa: In a hotel in Nice he writes a will, a set of farewell letters, and a chronicle of his own life, and prepares to kill himself. The month of it is nowhere fixed in the record. He is forty, divorced, without a post, and watching the German press close to him one paper at a time. He does not go through with it. He goes on to Ibiza, and then back to Germany for a few months more, and the will and the letters stay in his papers. What stopped him is not recorded in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The 1932 will and farewell letters, in the Walter Benjamin Archiv

stops.name: Paris, the exile begins
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1933 by both the German and English Wikipedia articles; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01. The pool's geography lens gave March 1933, which is unsupported by the source it cited and is not used. The pin is the Paris coordinate the corpus already uses.
stops.campa: In September he leaves Germany and does not go back. Paris is the base: the language he reads best after his own, the library he needs, a colony of German exiles arguing in cafés over how long this will last. He is stateless in practice long before he is stateless in law, living on stipends, small commissions, and the hospitality of people not much better off than he is. He publishes under pseudonyms in German papers for as long as that is still possible, because the fees are the difference between a room and no room. The Arcades notes and the Klee come with him.
suggested_refs: Benjamin's Paris addresses of the exile years, catalogued in the Walter Benjamin Archiv

stops.name: Sanremo, the pension his ex-wife runs
stops.date_confidence: the stays across the 1930s are attested; no single visit is dated and the year here only orders the segment. The pin is the town centre of Sanremo: German Wikipedia identifies the house as the Villa Emily, also called Villa Verde, formerly the residence of Edward Lear, but its address was not established in this pass and the stop should be read as Sanremo rather than as the villa.
stops.campa: Dora has left Germany too and runs a house at Sanremo as a pension, the Villa Emily, also called the Villa Verde, once the residence of the English painter Edward Lear. Her former husband stays there for long stretches through the exile years: a divorced man lodging with the woman who divorced him, because there is nowhere cheaper and nobody else who will take him for months at a time. He works there while she feeds the guests. Stefan is moving between schools in two countries.
suggested_refs: The Villa Emily / Villa Verde at Sanremo, run by Dora Sophie Kellner

stops.name: Skovsbostrand, the summers at Brecht's farmhouse
stops.date_confidence: visits are attested across 1934-1938; sources give summer for the first and the day is not fixed. The pin is Skovsbostrand 8, Brecht's rented house, geocoded by Nominatim; the pool's coordinate sat about 4.5 kilometres away in Svendborg town.
stops.campa: He takes the ferry north to the Danish coast at Skovsbostrand, where Bertolt Brecht has rented a thatched farmhouse under an enormous flat sky, and stays for months at a stretch across several summers. They play chess, mostly in silence, and argue over whether Benjamin's way of writing is a Marxist practice or a mystical one in working clothes. Brecht calls the Kafka essay Jewish fascism. Benjamin writes the remark down in his notes on the conversations and comes back the following year.
suggested_refs: Benjamin, 'Gespräche mit Brecht', the Svendborg conversation notes
Skovsbostrand 8, Svendborg, Brecht's Danish exile house

segments.name: Paris, the Institute, and the Camp

stops.name: Paris, the work of art essay in the Zeitschrift
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1936 for the French publication in the Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung; month and day default to 01. The essay exists in several versions and the printed French text is not the one Benjamin submitted.
stops.campa: The essay on the work of art in the age of its technical reproducibility appears in French in the Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung, the journal of Max Horkheimer's Institute for Social Research, itself in exile and running its affairs out of New York. The Institute pays Benjamin a monthly stipend that is the difference between working and not eating. The price is editorial: the printed version has been negotiated, cut, and softened exactly where its politics are most exposed. He signs it anyway.
stops.quote: the unique phenomenon of a distance, however close it may be
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935), trans. Harry Zohn: the definition of aura
suggested_refs: 'L'oeuvre d'art à l'époque de sa reproduction mécanisée', Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung, 1936
sources: marxists.org transcription of the Zohn translation

stops.name: Paris, the Collège de Sociologie and Georges Bataille
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives a 1937-1939 span for his contact with the Collège de Sociologie; the year here opens that span and month and day default to 01. The pin is the Paris coordinate the corpus already uses.
stops.campa: He attends the Collège de Sociologie, the group around Georges Bataille, Roger Caillois, and Michel Leiris that meets to discuss the sacred, sacrifice, and the founding force of myth in modern society. He listens, and he objects. What the group treats as a research programme he reads as the same operation the regime is running at Nuremberg, the aestheticizing of politics, carried out by intellectuals who believe their own irony makes them immune to it. Bataille will nonetheless be the man he trusts with his papers.
stops.quote: The logical result of Fascism is the introduction of aesthetics into political life.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935), trans. Harry Zohn, closing section
suggested_refs: Denis Hollier, ed., Le Collège de Sociologie 1937-1939
sources: marxists.org transcription of the Zohn translation

stops.name: Paris, the Baudelaire sent back
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1938 for Adorno's rejection of the first version, with the rewritten essay appearing in 1939; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Adorno reads the first version of Das Paris des Second Empire bei Baudelaire and sends it back. The objection is that Benjamin has laid economic facts beside poems without the mediation of theory, that the wine tax and the flâneur are juxtaposed rather than dialectically related, and that the result is closer to astonishment than to argument. Benjamin does not concede the principle, and the Institute goes on paying while the two of them argue it out by post. He rewrites. Über einige Motive bei Baudelaire appears in the Zeitschrift the following year.
suggested_refs: The Adorno-Benjamin correspondence, 1938-1940
'Über einige Motive bei Baudelaire', Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung, 1939

stops.name: Paris, 10 rue Dombasle
stops.date_confidence: the address and the span 1938-1940 are attested by English Wikipedia. The pin is Nominatim's geocoding of 10 rue Dombasle, 75015; the pool's coordinate sat about 230 metres off. Month and day default to 01, putting this stop on the same nominal date as the Baudelaire rejection.
stops.campa: His last settled address is a small rented room at 10 rue Dombasle in the fifteenth arrondissement, with a table, a bed, and the Klee on the wall. Possessions go to the pawnshop in rotation and come back when a payment arrives. Other exiles come up in the evenings to play cards. Every letter of these two years contains a sentence about the manuscripts: where they are, who holds copies, what would become of the Arcades convolutes if he had to leave in a hurry.
suggested_refs: 10 rue Dombasle, Paris 15e, Benjamin's last settled address

stops.name: Varennes-Vauzelles, the camp near Nevers
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1939 for the internment and November 1939 for the release; the day is not fixed. Two names for the site stand in the sources: German Wikipedia gives the Château de Vernuche at Varennes-Vauzelles, the pool's other source gives a Clos Saint-Joseph near Nevers, which could not be sourced at all in this pass. The better-attested name is pinned and the disagreement is not resolved.
stops.campa: France, at war with Germany, interns its German refugees as enemy aliens. Benjamin, forty-seven and in bad health, is sent to a camp in a half-finished château north of Nevers and held there roughly three months, sleeping on straw. Two names for the place stand in the record, the Château de Vernuche at Varennes-Vauzelles and a Clos Saint-Joseph nobody has been able to find. He organizes a lecture course for the other internees. French writers petition on his behalf and he is released in November. Germany has meanwhile stripped him of his citizenship. He returns to Paris stateless.
suggested_refs: Akademie der Künste, 'Passport issued to Walter Benjamin', archive record
sources: Akademie der Künste, adk.de/en/archives, passport record

stops.name: Paris, Über den Begriff der Geschichte
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1940; the theses are usually dated to the spring, before the flight from Paris in June, and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: In the last spring, in a Paris that is expecting the German army, he writes eighteen theses and two addenda on the concept of history: against progress, against the faith of social democracy in the current of events, against historicism's habit of feeling its way into the position of the victors. He tells Gretel Adorno the text is not for publication, that it would be handed straight over to enthusiastic misunderstanding. He gives a copy to Hannah Arendt before he leaves the city.
stops.quote: To articulate what is past does not mean to recognize 'how it really was.' It means to take control of a memory, as it flashes in a moment of danger.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'On the Concept of History' (1940), Thesis VI, trans. Dennis Redmond, marxists.org
suggested_refs: Über den Begriff der Geschichte, 1940, first published by the Institute in 1942
sources: marxists.org archive edition of the theses

stops.name: Paris, the papers left with Georges Bataille
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1940, immediately before the flight south; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01. The pin is the Bibliothèque nationale's Richelieu site, where Bataille worked; the Tolbiac building sometimes cited for this episode did not exist until 1996.
stops.campa: Before the flight he divides the papers. The Arcades convolutes, thousands of pages of quotation and commentary built over thirteen years, go to Georges Bataille, who is a librarian at the Bibliothèque nationale and hides them inside the building, where they sit out the occupation. Copies of other work go to Hannah Arendt, who will carry them to New York. He takes almost nothing out himself. The Klee stays on the wall of the flat in the fifteenth arrondissement and comes through the war there.
stops.quote: There has never been a document of culture, which is not simultaneously one of barbarism.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'On the Concept of History' (1940), Thesis VII, trans. Dennis Redmond, marxists.org
suggested_refs: The Arcades papers recovered from the Bibliothèque nationale after the war
sources: Verso Books blog on the Angelus Novus provenance

stops.name: Lourdes, the waiting town
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 June 1940 for the departure from Paris toward Lourdes, the day before the Germans entered the city; the stay runs into July.
stops.campa: He leaves Paris a day before the German army enters it, on trains packed with people going anywhere south, and comes to rest at Lourdes among refugees quartered in a pilgrimage town that has beds because no pilgrims are coming. Around him a place organized entirely around one miracle fills up with people waiting for another. He has no papers to go further, and writes to New York about the visa the Institute is trying to obtain for him. The stay runs on into July.
suggested_refs: Benjamin's letters from Lourdes, June-July 1940

stops.name: Marseille, the visa without the exit permit
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1940 for the American entry visa obtained at Marseille; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The American visa comes through and he goes to Marseille to use it, into a port holding thousands of people with the same document and the same problem. He has the United States entry visa and transit visas for Spain and Portugal. He does not have the French exit permit, and Vichy will not issue one to a German. A plan to leave by sea collapses in the harbour. Behind him the armistice has committed France to surrender named refugees on demand, which makes the whole coast a waiting room with a clock in it. What remains is to cross the border without permission, on foot, over the Pyrenees.
suggested_refs: Varian Fry and the Emergency Rescue Committee in Marseille, 1940-41

stops.name: Banyuls-sur-Mer, the black briefcase
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 September 1940 for the crossing; the account of the party and the briefcase comes from Lisa Fittko's memoir as summarized in the secondary literature, which is the only witness for most of the detail.
stops.campa: At Banyuls-sur-Mer, the last French town before the mountains, Lisa Fittko is running refugees over the border on a route the local mayor has described to her. Benjamin joins a small party: Henny Gurland and her teenage son. He has a heart condition and he is carrying a heavy black briefcase which he will not set down and which he tells Fittko matters more than he does. Nobody who saw it wrote down what was in it. That evening they walk part of the ridge to fix the route, and sleep in the open.
suggested_refs: Lisa Fittko, Mein Weg über die Pyrenäen
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Walter Benjamin', summarizing Fittko

stops.name: The Coll de Rumpissa, the crossing on foot
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The general course of the route between Banyuls and Portbou is attested, but its exact historical waypoints are not, and the coordinate is a point on the ridge rather than a documented location. The modern marked path is a later reconstruction with its own mapping choices.
stops.campa: The climb starts before dawn. A path over these hills is marked and walked now as the Chemin Walter Benjamin, laid out over ground nobody surveyed at the time. Fittko takes the party over the ridge and down toward Portbou across a day of vineyard terraces, scree, and open rock, Benjamin resting ten minutes in every hour on a schedule he sets himself and holds to, the briefcase always with him. Nobody in the party carries papers that would survive a check. They cross in the afternoon and come down into the town from above, seeing the bay before they see the border post.
suggested_refs: The Chemin Walter Benjamin, marked route Banyuls-sur-Mer to Portbou
sources: Lisa Fittko's account as summarized by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

stops.name: Portbou, the night at the Hotel de Francia
stops.date_confidence: the death date is contested and the contradiction is left standing: the English and German Wikipedia articles give 26 September 1940, while the Portbou civil register, certificate no. 25, and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy give 27 September. The hotel no longer operates and could not be geocoded, so the pin is the town of Portbou; the pool's coordinate sat some 800 metres south of the built-up town and is not used.
stops.campa: At the Spanish border post the party is told that a recent order bars refugees without French exit visas, that they will be handed back to France in the morning, and that they may spend the night in the town under guard. They take rooms at the Hotel de Francia. In the night Benjamin swallows the morphine tablets he has carried since Marseille and gives Henny Gurland a message for Adorno. A doctor is called and treats him for a stroke. The rest of the party is let through into Spain the following day, the order having been reversed or ignored, and goes on to Lisbon.
stops.quote: In a situation presenting no way out, I have no other choice but to make an end of it. It is in a small village in the Pyrenees, where no one knows me, that my life will come to a close.
stops.quote_source: The farewell note transcribed by Henny Gurland for Theodor Adorno, in Benjamin, Selected Writings vol. 4 (Harvard/Belknap); Gurland destroyed the original after reading it and wrote this version down later from memory, so no autograph exists
suggested_refs: Howard Eiland and Michael W. Jennings, Walter Benjamin: A Critical Life
Bruno Tackels, Walter Benjamin: Une vie dans les textes
sources: University of Chicago Press excerpt on the Portbou records, press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/790045.ht

stops.name: Portbou, the entry in the register
stops.date_confidence: attested. The University of Chicago Press excerpt reproduces certificate no. 25, dated 27 September 1940. The pin is a town-hall approximation for Portbou, not a surveyed address.
stops.campa: The town registers the death as certificate number twenty-five: Benjamin Walter, forty-eight years old, of Berlin, cause of death cerebral apoplexy, religion Roman Catholic. The name is inverted, no autopsy is performed, and almost every particular of the entry apart from the age and the city is wrong or unknowable. The hotel presents its bill for the four-day stay: the room, five sodas with lemon, four telephone calls, the dressing of the corpse, the disinfection of the room.
suggested_refs: Portbou civil register, death certificate no. 25, 27 September 1940
David Mauas, Who Killed Walter Benjamin?, 2005
sources: University of Chicago Press excerpt on the Portbou records, press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/790045.ht

stops.name: Portbou, the rented niche in the Catholic cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested. The University of Chicago Press excerpt gives Henny Gurland's payment of 28 September 1940 and the priest's receipt of 1 October for 96 pesetas. The pin is Nominatim's geocoding of the Cementiri de Portbou; the pool carried two different coordinates for this site, one about 500 metres off and one about 1.1 kilometres off, and neither is used.
stops.campa: Henny Gurland pays a priest ninety-six pesetas: six for a mass, seventy-five for five years' rent of a niche in the Catholic cemetery on the slope above the sea. A carpenter's receipt survives for a coffin lined with cloth, and a bricklayer's for eight pesetas to close the niche. Because the register had entered him as a Catholic, he lies in consecrated ground he had no claim on. The rental runs out after five years and nobody renews it. Where in that cemetery he was put is not now known.
stops.quote: For in it every second was the narrow gate, through which the Messiah could enter.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'On the Concept of History' (1940), Addendum B, the final line of the theses; trans. Dennis Redmond, marxists.org
suggested_refs: Dani Karavan, Passages, inaugurated 15 May 1994 beside the Portbou cemetery
Michael Taussig, Walter Benjamin's Grave, University of Chicago Press, 2005/2006
sources: University of Chicago Press excerpt on the Portbou records
Fundació Angelus Novus, memorial page, fundacioangelusnovus.org/en/memorial/

stops.name: Jerusalem, the angel by the terms of the will
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1987 for the donation to the Israel Museum by Fania Scholem; month and day default to 01. The route from the Paris flat through Theodor Adorno in New York to Gershom Scholem in Jerusalem is attested in outline by the Angelus Novus provenance record, though its individual dates are not.
stops.campa: By the terms of the will the Klee monoprint goes to Gershom Scholem. It reaches him after the war by way of Adorno in New York and hangs in the Scholem flat in Jerusalem for four decades; in 1987 Fania Scholem gives it to the Israel Museum, in the city Benjamin promised for twenty-five years to come to and never saw. It is the object he kept longest, and the one piece of his estate that was always meant to end up here. The angel is small. It is not looking at anyone, and its wings are up.
stops.quote: But a storm is blowing from Paradise, it has caught itself up in his wings and is so strong that the Angel can no longer close them. The storm drives him irresistibly into the future, to which his back is turned, while the rubble-heap before him grows sky-high. That which we call progress, is this storm.
stops.quote_source: Walter Benjamin, 'On the Concept of History' (1940), Thesis IX, trans. Dennis Redmond, marxists.org
suggested_refs: Paul Klee, Angelus Novus, 1920, Israel Museum, Jerusalem
Verso Books, 'The Storm Blowing from Paradise'
